terms.p: A method such as map or filter that returns a new iterator wrapping the old one and does no work at all until something asks it for an element.
terms.x: an iterator that wraps an iterator

terms.p: Having more than one path to the same piece of memory, which is harmless on its own and dangerous the moment one of those paths can write.
terms.x: two ways to reach one value

terms.p: A cost that is occasionally large but averages out small across a run of operations, which is why growing a Vec one push at a time is still linear overall.
A crate giving applications a single boxed error type that any error converts into, plus a chain of context strings for the human reading the message.
Rc with an atomic counter, so it can be shared across threads. Slightly slower, and the only one that is Send.
A function defined in an impl block that takes no self parameter, so it is called through the type rather than through a value, as in Config::new.
A type named inside a trait that each implementing type fixes exactly once, such as the Item an iterator yields.
terms.x: one type chosen by the implementor

terms.p: Syntax that turns a function into a state machine returning a Future, so the thread can do something else while it waits.
An operation the hardware guarantees no other core can observe halfway through, which is how a counter can be shared without a lock.
Traits like Send and Sync that nobody writes an impl for: the compiler decides a type has them if every one of its fields does.
terms.x: traits the compiler implements for you

terms.p: What a bounded channel gives you: once it is full the sender blocks, so a fast producer cannot pile up unbounded work for a slow consumer.
terms.x: a full queue slowing the producer

terms.p: Tony Hoare's name for adding a null reference to a language in 1965, so called because absence and presence share one type and the check is never forced.
A name introduced by `let` and attached to a value, immutable unless declared `mut` and live until the end of its scope.
Whether the names introduced by a pattern take the matched data itself or a reference to it, which the compiler chooses based on whether you matched on a value or on a reference.
Implementing a trait for every type satisfying some bound at once, such as impl<T: Display> ToString for T.
Taking a reference to a value: permission to use it without owning it. The value cannot be moved or dropped while the borrow is live.
The compiler pass that verifies every reference is valid for as long as it is used and that no two conflicting borrows overlap.
The simplest owning pointer: it puts a value on the heap and frees it when dropped. Used for recursive types and for trait objects.
Receiving a value itself rather than a reference to it, which transfers ownership to the receiver.
How many elements a Vec or String has room for before it must reallocate — always at least its length, usually more.
A variable from the surrounding scope that a closure stores in its generated struct, either as a reference or as an owned value.
Rust's build system and package manager: it resolves dependencies, compiles, tests, benchmarks and publishes.
A tool that prints your crate with every macro expanded, so generated code can be read as ordinary Rust.
A wrapper allowing a value to be replaced through a shared reference by only ever copying whole values in and out, so no reference to the inside ever escapes.
A byte position in a string that sits at the start of a character rather than in the middle of one, which is the only kind of position a string slice is allowed to begin or end at.
terms.x: a byte offset you may slice at

terms.p: A cargo subcommand that runs several hundred lints beyond the compiler's own, mostly about idiom and needless work.
An explicit duplicate via .clone(), which may allocate. Unlike Copy it never happens implicitly, so the cost is always visible in the source.
An anonymous function that captures variables from its surrounding scope, by reference or by value depending on what it does with them.
The restriction that a trait impl must be in the crate defining either the trait or the type, so two crates cannot supply conflicting impls.
A small method that takes a value and a closure and hands back a new value of the same shape, letting you describe a transformation without writing out the match by hand.
terms.x: a method that transforms without unpacking

terms.p: A generic parameter that is a compile-time value rather than a type, most often the length N in an array type [T; N].
A method such as collect, sum or count that calls next until the iterator is finished, which is the only point at which any of the work happens.
terms.x: the thing that actually runs the chain

terms.p: A marker meaning a value can be duplicated by copying its bytes, so assignment leaves the original usable. Only for types that own nothing needing cleanup.
The rule that a reference valid for a long region may be used wherever one valid for a shorter region is wanted.
The unit the compiler builds at once: either a library or a binary. A package may contain several.
The public registry cargo downloads dependencies from, where every published version of a crate stays available forever.
A stretch of code during which interrupts are disabled, so that shared data cannot be modified halfway through by a handler.
A reference to memory that no longer holds the value it was made from. Rust rejects these at compile time rather than crashing on them.
Two threads touching the same memory at the same time with at least one writing. Rust's borrow rules make this a compile error.
Two or more threads each holding a lock the other needs, so none of them can ever continue.
terms.x: two threads waiting on each other

terms.p: A macro defined by pattern-matching rules over syntax rather than by arbitrary code.
A method a trait supplies a body for, so every implementor gets it free and only overrides it when it has a faster way.
terms.x: a trait method that comes pre-written

terms.p: The trait a type implements to say what it points at, which is what makes the star operator and method lookup reach through it.
terms.x: the trait behind the star operator

terms.p: The compiler silently converting a reference to a pointer-like type into a reference to what it points at, repeatedly, until the expected type is reached.
The simpler form a piece of convenient syntax expands into before the compiler type-checks it.
The small hidden number stored inside an enum value that says which variant it currently is.
The rule since edition 2021 that a closure captures the individual struct fields its body mentions rather than the whole struct.
An expression that does not produce a value because control leaves instead, by returning, breaking, continuing or panicking.
A code block in a documentation comment, which cargo test extracts, compiles as a separate crate against your library, and executes.
Returning the same allocation to the allocator twice. It corrupts the allocator's bookkeeping and is a reliable route from a memory bug to an exploit.
The automatic cleanup that runs when an owner goes out of scope: it releases the value's resources, freeing heap memory, closing files, unlocking mutexes.
A hidden boolean the compiler inserts when it cannot tell statically whether a value was moved, so it knows at runtime whether to drop it. Usually optimised away.
Looking up which function to call through a vtable at runtime. What trait objects give you, at the cost of an indirection.
A named opt-in set of language changes, such as 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024. Crates on different editions interoperate freely.
The compiler filling in lifetime names in a function signature using three fixed rules, so that most signatures need no annotation at all.
terms.x: the lifetimes rustc writes for you

terms.p: HashMap::entry, which hands you the slot for a key whether or not anything is in it, so look-up-then-insert-then-update costs a single hash.
A type that is exactly one of several named variants, each able to carry its own data. Far more useful than a C enum.
The stable identifier printed in square brackets after the word error, which you can look up with rustc --explain.
A short description attached to an error as it passes up through a layer, so the final message says which file was being read rather than only that something was missing.
terms.x: what you were trying to do

terms.p: The official page listing every rustc error code with a minimal broken example and a fixed one, the same text rustc --explain prints.
The library component that holds a queue of tasks and polls them; Rust ships none, so you pick tokio or another runtime.
Describing a match that handles every value the scrutinee could possibly be, which the compiler checks and refuses to compile without.
The requirement that a match covers every possible case, which turns adding an enum variant into a compile error at every place that must change.
Any piece of code that evaluates to a value, which in Rust is almost everything including if, match, loop and a block in braces.
A pointer carrying a second word of metadata — a length for slices, a vtable address for trait objects.
Calling code written in another language, which is always unsafe because the compiler cannot see what that code does.
The trait for a closure whose body only reads what it captured, so it can be called from several places at once.
The trait for a closure whose body changes something it captured, so it needs unique access each call.
The trait for a closure whose body consumes something it captured, so calling it destroys it.
The label after a metavariable in a macro matcher saying what kind of syntax it accepts, and therefore where in the output it may be used.
The trait a collection implements to say it can be built out of an iterator, which is what lets collect produce a Vec, a String, a HashMap or a Result.
The problem that async code can call ordinary code but not the reverse, so making one function async tends to force every caller to become async too.
The type written fn(i32) -> i32, a single word holding the address of some code, with no room for captured variables.
Wrapping an iterator so that once it has returned None it keeps returning None, which the trait itself does not promise.
A value representing work that is not finished. It does nothing until polled, which is why an async function that is never awaited never runs.
Code written against a type parameter rather than a concrete type, specialised by the compiler for each type actually used.
The one type a program nominates to serve every heap allocation, which a program without an operating system has to supply itself.
A range that includes its start and excludes its end, so its length is always the end minus the start and adjacent ranges never overlap.
The small fixed-size struct that lives on the stack and points at heap contents — for a String, the pointer, length and capacity.
terms.x: the stack part of a heap value

terms.p: Memory requested at runtime for values whose size or lifetime the stack cannot accommodate. Someone must decide when to give it back; in Rust the owner does.
The rule that an identifier written inside a macro is resolved where the macro was defined, so it can neither capture nor be captured by a name at the call site.
Syntax standing for some single concrete type satisfying a trait, used as shorthand for a type parameter in an argument and to return a type that has no name.
terms.x: an unnamed type meeting a bound

terms.p: A test file under tests/, compiled as its own crate, which can only see the public API of your library — the same view an outside user gets.
Mutating through a shared reference, with the borrow rule moved from compile time to runtime and enforced by a panic instead of an error.
The trait that says a value can be turned into an iterator, which is the only thing a for loop knows how to consume.
terms.x: what a for loop asks for

terms.p: A position in a type where no other lifetime may be swapped in, in either direction, because the value can be both read and written through it.
A value producing items one at a time via next(). Lazy by construction: adapters build a description, and nothing runs until something consumes it.
A reference or iterator into a collection left pointing at freed memory because the collection grew and moved its contents elsewhere.
terms.x: the reference that outlived its buffer

terms.p: The value thread::spawn gives back, whose join method waits for that thread to finish and hands you what it returned.
terms.x: a handle to a running thread

terms.p: A break that names an enclosing loop or block, so it exits that one rather than the innermost one.
Building a description of a computation and doing none of it until a result is demanded, so work that is never needed is never performed.
A let that binds a pattern when it matches and otherwise runs a block that must leave the function, so the binding is usable in everything that follows.
A named region of code over which a reference is guaranteed valid. It describes a claim the compiler checks, not a duration you set.
The rules that let you omit lifetime annotations in common function signatures, because the compiler can infer the only sensible answer.
The flag a mutex sets when a thread panics while holding it, so later lockers are told the data may have been left half-updated.
Optimising across crate boundaries at link time instead of one crate at a time, which lets the compiler inline and delete code it otherwise could not see.
Code that writes code, expanded before type checking. Declarative macros match on syntax; procedural macros run arbitrary Rust at compile time.
The rule that matching a reference against an ordinary pattern quietly borrows instead of failing, so every name the pattern binds comes out as a reference and nothing is moved.
An extra condition written after a pattern that must also be true for the arm to be chosen, and which the exhaustiveness check deliberately ignores.
The pattern a macro rule matches its arguments against, written in tokens rather than types.
Memory that stays allocated with nothing able to reach it, which wastes space but is not unsafe, so Rust permits it in safe code.
A name in a macro pattern that binds whatever syntax matched at that position, then stands in for it in the generated code.
An interpreter that runs Rust at the intermediate-representation level and reports undefined behaviour that ordinary testing cannot see.
A named namespace inside a crate, controlling which items are visible outside it.
The nested arrangement of modules inside one crate, rooted at src/main.rs or src/lib.rs and built out by mod declarations rather than by the filesystem.
The compiler emitting one specialised copy of a generic function per concrete type used, which is why generic Rust costs nothing at runtime.
To emit a specialised copy of generic code for each concrete type it is used with.
Transferring ownership from one binding to another. It copies the small fixed-size handle, not the heap contents, and the old binding becomes unusable.
Transferring ownership from one binding to another. It copies the small fixed-size handle, not the heap contents, and the old binding becomes unusable.
A unique borrow that permits mutation. Exactly one may exist at a time, and no shared reference may coexist with it.
The value a lock call returns, which gives access to the data inside the mutex and releases the lock when it is dropped.
terms.x: proof that you hold the lock

terms.p: The type of an expression that never hands control back, such as panic! or return, which is allowed to stand in for any type because no value of it can ever exist.
A single-field tuple struct wrapping another type, used to add meaning or to implement a foreign trait without breaking coherence.
A bit pattern a type can never legally hold, which the compiler is free to reuse to mean something else, such as the empty case of an Option.
The compiler using a bit pattern the payload can never hold, such as a null pointer, to stand for a variant, so the enum needs no separate tag and takes no extra space.
The rule, since the 2018 edition, that a borrow lasts until the last place it is used rather than until the end of the block it was created in.
terms.x: a borrow ends at its last use

terms.p: A trait whose every method can be reached through a table of function pointers, which rules out generic methods, methods with no self, and methods returning Self by value.
The set of conditions a trait must meet before values of it can be used behind dyn, mainly that every method has a receiver and no type parameters of its own.
A value that is either Some(T) or None. Rust's replacement for null, and the compiler makes you handle the empty case.
Several patterns joined with a vertical bar so one arm handles all of them, which requires every alternative to bind the same names at the same types.
You may only implement a trait for a type if you defined one of the two, so that no two crates can claim the same implementation.
The single binding responsible for a value. When it goes out of scope the value is dropped, which is how Rust knows when to free memory without a garbage collector.
A directory with a Cargo.toml that Cargo can build, test and publish, holding at most one library crate and any number of binary crates.
An unrecoverable failure that unwinds the stack, running destructors as it goes. For bugs, not for expected error conditions.
The single function a program without the standard library must provide to say what happens when code panics, since there is no default.
Destructuring a value by its shape and binding its parts, checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler.
A wrapper saying the value behind it will stay at one address forever, which is what makes it safe for a future to hold a pointer into itself.
terms.x: a promise not to move a value

terms.p: The two-variant enum a future's poll method returns: Ready with the final value, or Pending meaning ask again after the waker fires.
The small set of standard library names the compiler injects into every module automatically, which is why Option and Vec need no use line.
The part of your code a diagnostic underlines with carets, marking where the compiler stopped — which is not always where the mistake is.
A compile-time function taking a stream of tokens and returning a stream of tokens, which must live in its own crate.
Testing by stating a rule that should hold for every input and letting a tool search for a counterexample, then shrink it to the smallest case that still fails.
terms.x: assert a law, not an example

terms.p: The record of which allocation and which permission a pointer was derived from, which is part of whether using it is legal even when the address is right.
Tying a resource to a value's lifetime, so acquiring the value acquires the resource and dropping it releases the resource — no cleanup code at every exit.
An address with no guarantees attached: it may be null, may point at freed memory, and nothing tracks what else points at the same place.
A reference-counted shared owner for single-threaded code. The value is dropped when the last Rc goes away.
A pub use line that makes an item reachable by a name other than the one its own module gives it, which is how a crate's public API is kept separate from its internal layout.
terms.x: publishing an item at a new path

terms.p: Asking the allocator for a larger block, copying every element into it and freeing the old one, which is what a Vec does when it runs out of capacity.
A shorter borrow taken through an existing mutable reference, which freezes the original for its duration and then hands it back.
The self parameter of a method, whose form — &self, &mut self or self — decides whether calling it reads the value, writes to it, or consumes it.
A failure that a correct program will meet in normal operation and that the caller can sensibly act on, which is what Result is for.
The maximum depth of nested macro expansions the compiler will perform before giving up.
A container that enforces the borrow rules at runtime instead of compile time, panicking if you break them.
A pointer the compiler guarantees is valid and non-null for as long as you can use it. Shared (&T) or unique (&mut T), never both at once.
Two or more reference-counted values holding handles to each other, so each keeps the other's count above zero and neither is ever freed.
The set of points in your code over which a reference has to stay valid; a lifetime name like 'a is a name for one of these, not a length of time.
A macro construct that matches a group any number of times and emits its body once per match, which is how a macro takes a variable number of arguments.
An attribute fixing how a type is laid out in memory, needed whenever another language has to agree about where the fields are.
A value that is either Ok(T) or Err(E). Errors are ordinary return values, so ignoring one is visible in the source.
Bindings in a scope are dropped last-declared-first, because later values are the ones most likely to depend on earlier ones.
One fixed allocation with a head and a tail index that wrap around to the start, giving constant-time insertion and removal at both ends without shifting anything.
The standard code formatter, run as `cargo fmt`, which has one style and almost no options so that every Rust codebase looks the same.
A safe interface built over unsafe operations, where the wrapper itself checks whatever the compiler could not.
A comment above an unsafe block stating which precondition it relies on and why that precondition holds at that point.
A thread started inside thread::scope, which the compiler knows will be joined before the scope ends, so it may borrow local variables.
terms.x: a thread that cannot outlive its scope

terms.p: A place the compiler underlines with dashes because it participates in the error, such as the earlier borrow that made a later one illegal.
The convention that a version number says how much a release broke, so a change to anything publicly reachable forces a new major version.
A marker meaning a value is safe to move to another thread. Almost everything is; Rc is the notable exception.
Declaring a new binding with the same name as an existing one. The old value still exists; the name simply refers to the new one.
A read-only borrow. Many may exist at once, and none of them may mutate what they point at.
The hash function a Rust HashMap uses by default, seeded randomly at startup so that an attacker cannot craft keys that all collide.
A borrowed view of a contiguous run of elements: a pointer plus a length, pointing into something someone else owns.
A value that points at something, owns it, and does extra work when it is dropped — freeing a buffer, decrementing a count, releasing a lock.
terms.x: a pointer that owns and cleans up

terms.p: The property that no possible use of a safe API can cause undefined behaviour; an API that can be broken by an ordinary caller is unsound.
Borrowing two different fields of the same value at once, which is allowed because the compiler tracks each field path separately.
Per-call memory, pushed on entry and popped on return. Fast, and only usable for values whose size is known at compile time.
The enum the compiler builds from an async function, with one variant per await point holding exactly the variables that must survive it.
terms.x: what an async fn compiles into

terms.p: A piece of code that does something without producing a value; Rust has only two, a let binding and an item declaration.
Resolving which function to call at compile time, so the call can be inlined. What generics give you.
A mutable global variable with no synchronisation, so any two threads touching it are a data race and therefore undefined behaviour.
A borrowed view of UTF-8 bytes. It can point into a String, into a literal in the binary, or into part of either.
A growable, heap-allocated, UTF-8 string that owns its buffer. The owned counterpart to &str.
Writing ..other at the end of a struct literal to take every field you did not list from another value of the same type, moving each one that is not Copy.
A type whose values are exactly one of a listed set of shapes, so the number of possible values is the sum of the alternatives rather than the product of a set of fields.
A trait named after a colon in another trait's declaration, meaning anything implementing the second must also implement the first.
An await inside an async function: the one kind of place where the task can give control back and be resumed later.
terms.x: a place a future can pause

terms.p: A marker meaning a value is safe to reference from several threads at once — equivalently, that &T is Send.
The last expression in a block, written without a semicolon, whose value becomes the value of the whole block.
The string naming an architecture, operating system and ABI, such as thumbv7em-none-eabihf, where none means there is no operating system.
terms.x: the platform you are building for

terms.p: The hidden entry point the compiler builds from every function marked with the test attribute, which runs them in parallel and reports the results.
Shorthand that returns early with the error if a Result is Err, and otherwise unwraps the Ok value.
A crate that generates the Display and Error impls for your own error enum, leaving the type concrete so callers can still match on its variants.
A single token, or a whole group enclosed in brackets treated as one unit, which is the coarsest thing a macro pattern can match.
The sequence of tokens a procedural macro receives and returns, carrying no type information at all.
A named set of methods a type can implement. Rust's answer to interfaces, and the basis of both generics and dynamic dispatch.
A constraint saying a type parameter must implement a given trait, which is what makes the parameter's methods callable.
A value behind a pointer whose concrete type is not known at compile time, carrying a vtable so calls can be dispatched at runtime.
The tokens a macro rule emits, with each metavariable replaced by whatever it matched.
Reading one type's bytes as another type, which is undefined behaviour unless every possible bit pattern is valid for the target.
The ::<Type> syntax for supplying type arguments explicitly where inference cannot decide, as in parse::<i32>().
A name written in angle brackets, such as the T in fn largest<T>, that stands for a type the caller picks rather than one you fixed in advance.
Encoding what stage a value is at in its type, so that calling a method too early or in the wrong order is a compile error rather than a runtime bug.
A state the language makes no promises about, where the compiler may assume it cannot happen and optimise accordingly. The thing safe Rust exists to prevent.
Any Unicode code point except the surrogate range, which is exactly what fits in Rust's four-byte char.
A type whose fields share one piece of storage, so reading a field asserts it is the field that was last written.
A test written in a child module beside the code, which can therefore reach private items the rest of the world cannot.
The type written (), which has exactly one value, takes up no space, and is what a function returns when it returns nothing.
A block where five extra operations are permitted, such as dereferencing a raw pointer. It does not disable the borrow checker; it moves responsibility for the invariants to you.
A trait whose correctness other code relies on for safety, so writing an impl requires the unsafe keyword and a stated justification.
What a panic does by default: it returns through every frame in turn, running the destructor of each live value, so locks are released and files are closed on the way out.
Reading memory that has already been handed back to the allocator, which may since have been given to something else entirely.
One of the named alternatives an enum value can be, together with whatever data that alternative carries.
A growable heap-allocated array that owns its elements: pointer, length and capacity, exactly like String.
How far an item can be reached from, ranging from the defining module alone up to every other crate.
terms.x: who is allowed to name this

terms.p: A table of function pointers carried alongside a trait object so the right implementation can be found at runtime.
The handle a future gives to whatever it is waiting on, so that when the data arrives the executor is told to poll that task again.
terms.x: the callback that says try again

terms.p: A reference-counted handle that does not keep the value alive, and which must be upgraded to a strong handle before use — returning nothing if the value has already gone.
terms.x: a handle that does not own

terms.p: The form that lists trait requirements after a function's return type instead of inside the angle brackets, and can constrain types you did not declare.
A set of packages sharing one lockfile, one build directory and one set of Cargo commands, so every member resolves to the same version of every dependency.
Marking a version on crates.io so no new project resolves to it, without deleting it — existing lockfiles keep building.
An abstraction that compiles to the same machine code you would have written by hand, so using it costs nothing at runtime.
